sentences.text: Compsognathus longipes was a tiny dinosaur, roughly the size of a modern chicken.
The German specimen stood about 70 to 75 centimeters tall and measured 89 centimeters long, while the French individual reached lengths between 1.25 and 1.4 meters.
Evidence from related species suggests the body may have been covered with feather-like structures.
A 2022 review interprets the skin impressions on the tail as aberrant bony growths rather than scales, noting they are texturally and mineralogically indistinguishable from the fossilized vertebrae.
Until the 1990s, Compsognathus was the smallest known dinosaur and the closest known relative of the primitive bird Archaeopteryx.
A 2007 computer model estimated that Compsognathus could reach a maximum speed of 17.8 m/s.

Excavators discovered 10mm diameter eggs near the fossil remains of the German specimen, though later researchers have doubted the assignment of these eggs to Compsognathus because they were found outside the animal's body cavity.
In 1993, Peter Griffiths interpreted circular irregularities on the German Compsognathus slab as immature eggs.
The genus Compsognathus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1875.
Paleontologists have found two well-preserved Compsognathus fossils, one in Germany in the 1850s and another in France discovered more than a century later.
The German Compsognathus specimen (BSP AS I 563) comes from limestone deposits in Bavaria and was part of the collection of Joseph Oberndorfer.
John Ostrom's thorough redescription in 1978 made Compsognathus one of the best-known small theropods to date.
The German specimen was found in lagoons situated between beaches and coral reefs on Jurassic European islands.
The diet of Compsognathus longipes is known with certainty from the remains of small, agile lizards preserved in the bellies of both specimens.
The lizard found in the stomach of the German Compsognathus specimen was identified as a new species named Schoenesmahl dyspepsia.
Ostrom identified the prey as a Bavarisaurus lizard, and biomechanical simulations suggest Compsognathus was an agile runner capable of reaching speeds near 64 km/h.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and others examined nine foot bones of Compsognathus for stress fractures but found none.
No other dinosaur fossils have been found with Compsognathus, suggesting it may have been the top land predator on its islands.
The German Compsognathus specimen is highly articulated, with disarticulation only seen in the skull, hands, cervical ribs, and gastralia.
The anaerobic bottom waters of the lagoon likely prevented scavengers from disturbing the Compsognathus carcass before burial.
The German specimen was found in lagoons situated between beaches and coral reefs on Jurassic European islands.
Compsognathus is classified in the family Compsognathidae.
Friedrich von Huene erected the infraorder Coelurosauria in 1914, which includes the Compsognathidae among other families of small theropods, and this classification has remained in use since.
During the Jurassic, the region where the German Compsognathus fossils were found was part of the Solnhofen archipelago.
The Compsognathidae, the group containing Compsognathus, lived during the late Jurassic and early Cretaceous periods in China, Europe, and South America.
Jens Zinke labeled forty-nine teeth from Portugal as Compsognathus sp. because they had serrations on the front edge and were not identical to those of Compsognathus longipes.
Bidar and colleagues argued in 1972 that the French specimen of Compsognathus had webbed hands that would have looked like flippers in life.
